summary: Gone tower in Iron County (FFLA list; Central U.S. Lookouts gives 44N-2E-20). No build, staffing or removal details for this site in sources checked; story uses statewide context.

facts.status_note: Listed as Gone by the Forest Fire Lookout Association; no source gives a removal date or method.

evidence.supports: Island Lake tower in Iron County at 46.27324, -90.27772; listed as Gone
Location given as Iron County, township 44N, range 2E, section 20
Statewide network, mostly in forested regions most prone to fire
evidence.quote: Wisconsin once had a vast fire tower lookout network, mostly in the forested and most fire prone regions of the state.

evidence.supports: 119 towers in use at the peak
evidence.quote: At the height of their use, 119 towers dotted the landscape.

evidence.supports: Steel frames made by the Aeromotor Company of Chicago, a maker of farm windmills
evidence.quote: These steel structures were manufactured by the Aeromotor Company in Chicago, which specialized in Windmills used on farms.

evidence.supports: Many surviving towers built in the 1930s by Civilian Conservation Corps workers
evidence.quote: Many of the towers we see still standing today were built during the 1930s by the young men of the Civilian Conservation Corps.

evidence.supports: Seasonal staffing May to September, later cut back to spring fire peak
evidence.quote: Manned from May to September for many decades, their staffing was reduced to the peak forest fire season, between snow melt and green up in the spring.

evidence.supports: 72 aging towers still in use decommissioned in 2015
evidence.quote: In 2015, the 72 aging towers still in use were decommissioned.
Built in the 1930's and 1940's, the towers at the time were the front line to protect Wisconsin's forests.

evidence.supports: Typical tower about 100 feet, steel, with 7-by-7 foot cab
evidence.quote: Towers are typically around 100 feet tall and made of steel with a 7-by-7 foot cab at the top.

evidence.supports: DNR announced the fire towers were being eliminated
evidence.quote: The DNR announced late last week the fire towers used to spot out of control fires were being eliminated.

evidence.supports: Cost of replacement and modern technology given as reasons
evidence.quote: the cost of replacing the towers and modern technology were factors in their demise

evidence.supports: Many DNR staffed towers on private property with easement rights
evidence.quote: many of which are located on private property with easement rights
As of last fall, the ownership of 37 towers was transferred to the private landowners on which the towers stand

evidence.supports: 10 sold and removed, 4 pending removal, 56 to dismantle
evidence.quote: 10 towers have been sold and removed, 4 are sold with removal pending, and 56 are left to dismantle

corrections.why: 44N is the township code from the land-survey location 44N-2E-20, not a managing agency. The Central U.S. Lookouts page names only Iron County and that code.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: WXPR says the towers were built in the 1930s and 1940s; WJFW says many surviving towers were built in the 1930s. Both describe the statewide network, and neither dates this tower.

notes_for_editor: Thin sourcing. Only the FFLA list (name, county, coordinates, Gone) and the Central U.S. Lookouts page (PLSS code 44N-2E-20) mention this tower; no build date, builder, height, staffing, removal or access record was found in two WebSearch queries and the cached pages. The story's built, staffing and fate paragraphs are statewide context from WJFW, WXPR and the FFLA 2019 chapter report, labelled as such. Brief correction: agency '44N' is a survey code. Conflict left open: the 2019 report's four categories total 107, while the 2015 reports say 72 towers were in use; the sources do not explain the gap. Check the Kent story, which gives the 2019 figures as 'as of fall 2019' where the report says 'as of last fall'. The Weebly page carries an image (3010051_orig.jpg) with no licence stated; not used. Leads: Iron County Historical Society (Hurley); Wisconsin Historical Society Architecture and History Inventory; WDNR fire tower divestment records; 1930s Wisconsin Conservation Bulletin; county land records for ownership before any access advice.
